title: Unit – 3 : Session – 3 : SLO – 1  |  Linked-List Stack — Advantages, Disadvantages, Applications
sections: I. Advantages of Pointer-Based Stacks
Stack implementation using pointers allows DYNAMIC memory allocation.
In pointer-based stacks, there is no need to define the MAXIMUM stack size.
Stack implemented using pointers can easily grow and SHRINK at runtime.
There is no WASTAGE of memory since space is allocated as needed.
Linked list-based stacks can handle a large number of elements until the system runs out of MEMORY.
Pointer-based stack avoids STACK overflow, unlike array-based stacks.
In pointer-based implementation, memory is released using FREE() when elements are popped.
Stacks using pointers are more FLEXIBLE for programs requiring flexible memory use.
No need to RESIZE (reallocate) the stack when it becomes full, unlike arrays.
Each node in a linked list-based stack contains both data and a POINTER to the next node.
II. Disadvantages of Pointer-Based Stacks
Stack implementation using pointers requires extra memory for storing POINTERS.
Each node in a linked list-based stack uses more MEMORY than array-based stacks.
Accessing elements in a pointer-based stack is SLOWER than in an array.
Stack operations in linked lists involve dynamic memory allocation, which can be COSTLY (slow).
Improper memory management in pointer-based stacks can lead to MEMORY leaks.
Debugging a pointer-based stack is more DIFFICULT than an array-based stack.
Pointer-based stack implementation depends on DYNAMIC allocation at runtime.
Excessive use of pointers increases the risk of RUNTIME (pointer) errors.
It is harder to determine the total number of elements without TRAVERSING through the stack.
Stack operations in pointer-based implementation are not as FAST (efficient) as array-based stacks for small data sets.
III. Applications
Stack using pointers is useful in handling VARIABLE (dynamic) size data efficiently.
Function call management in recursion uses a CALL stack.
Pointer-based stacks are suitable for evaluating and converting EXPRESSIONS (infix/postfix).
Stacks help in implementing UNDO and redo features in applications.
Pointer-based stacks are used in SYNTAX parsing for compilers.
Backtracking algorithms like maze solving or N-Queens use STACKS.
Stack using pointers is helpful in managing ACTIVATION (stack) frames in programming languages.
Depth-first search (DFS) in graphs can be implemented using a STACK.
Stacks are used in checking BALANCING of parentheses in expressions.
Linked list-based stacks are useful in systems with limited or unpredictable MEMORY availability.
